A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including the substantial additions in v4.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic-DAG experiments and concept-direction/probe alignment results on Pythia, Llama and DeepSeek models (Section 5 and Appendix H).

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds original SAE comparisons, ablations, validation controls and robustness results (Section 6 and Appendices I and N–R).

M1.justification: v2 has no SAE algorithm. v4 introduces structured SAEs with separate sparse and low-rank encoders, combined features z=S+R, and a reconstruction objective combining p-annealing sparsity with nuclear-norm regularization (Section 5 and Appendix I.1). This adds a substantive training method.

E1.justification: v4 adds SAE training on The Pile and evaluation of SAE reconstruction and concept recovery. Appendix R also evaluates eight additional semantic contrasts, including positive/negative, authentic/fake and toxic/neutral examples. The original simulations and 27 morphological, semantic and translation concept categories remain.

E2.justification: The new SAE comparisons actually evaluate top-k SAE (Gao et al., 2025), batch-top-k SAE (Bussmann et al., 2024) and p-annealing SAE (Karvonen et al., 2024) against structured SAE (Figure 4 and Tables 3–5). Appendices N and R additionally introduce probes trained with permuted labels as null comparators. These comparisons are absent from v2.

E3.justification: v4 adds 50%/50% separation of concept-direction estimation and probe fitting, 70%/30% probe testing, and SAE evaluation using Pearson correlation, Hungarian feature assignment and MSE. Table 1 revises reported word-pair counts, including country–capital from 15 to 158. These reported count changes do not establish that the unchanged original heatmaps were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 already studies observed-variable count and graph-structure sensitivity in Figure 2. v4 adds a low-rank coefficient sweep (Table 2), held-out and null controls, probe-quality analyses, regularization/class-weight/label-noise sensitivity, TV and concentration proxies, and tests on imperfect additional counterfactual pairs (Appendices N–R). These investigate substantial new robustness questions.

E5.justification: The five-run simulation protocol and its uncertainty plots are retained. v4 extends uncertainty reporting to SAE and real-LLM evaluations: three SAE trainings, ten-seed alignment heatmaps, three train/test splits with mean and standard deviation of probe accuracy, and five-seed results on additional semantic pairs (Appendices I and N–R).

E6.justification: The original simulation and alignment plots are retained, including v2 Figure 4 as v4 Figure 6. v4 adds substantial SAE, validation and sensitivity results. For example, Table 4 reports average Pythia-1.4b PCC of 0.752 ± 0.010 for structured SAE versus 0.742 ± 0.019 for p-annealing SAE. These are new comparisons, not improvements over v2 under matched settings.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 removes the requirement that the posterior-difference matrix and resulting transformation be square and invertible, distinguishes representation dimension from latent-state count, retains a constant bias, and adds TV and coverage conditions for the approximation. The corollaries are substantively revised using marginal posteriors and lifting matrices, with rewritten proofs and new binary-concept extensions (Appendices D–G).

C1.justification: v4 adds theoretically grounded SAE evaluation and structured SAEs to the central contributions. It narrows the abstract's transformation claim from an invertible linear transformation to a linear transformation. The introduction and conclusion reduce v2's assertions about deep understanding and emphasize representation interpretability and practical applications; causal-unmixing future directions remain in Appendix L.

C2.justification: v4 replaces the diversity-focused limitation with difficulty verifying the TV condition and elaborates the retained layer restriction for SAE applications. It adds a dependency-based explanation for low-rank regularization and discusses unreliable probing with scarce pairs, sensitivity to noisy supervision and imperfect counterfactuals. The earlier world-model discussion is retained in Appendix J.

D1.justification: Appendix I adds encoder equations, truncated-SVD implementation guidance, 32,768 SAE features, 20,000 training steps, batch size 10,000, optimizer and warm-up settings, the first 200 million Pile tokens, and four 40-GB A100 GPUs. v4 also adds a project link and a code-release promise; the PDFs do not establish that code has been released.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning through new discussions of SAEs, dictionary learning and structured sparsity in Appendix A. It also compares its scope with categorical/hierarchical concept modeling by Park et al. (2024) and multi-task identifiability by Zhang et al. (2025). These extend the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the main narrative is organized around setup, theory, insights and practice. Earlier future-direction discussion moves to Appendix L, while theorem explanations and appendix organization are substantially reworked. These changes exceed the insertion of new scientific content alone.

P2.justification: v4 adopts the ICLR layout and author block, revises Figure 1, enlarges the simulation display and relocates retained heatmaps. It adds SAE performance curves, detailed comparison tables, validation heatmaps and sensitivity plots. The Llama-3/DeepSeek heatmaps are retained as Figure 6 rather than being new results.

improvement.justification: v4's held-out and permuted-label controls address v2's reuse of the same supervision, while repeated-run analyses and implementation details improve empirical scrutiny. However, the expanded SAE contribution inconsistently identifies probe logits with probabilities (Appendix F, Eq. 71; Appendix I.2), whereas v2 used log-probabilities. Appendix Q also calls its concentration proxy small despite Table 6 reporting 0.7473. These issues leave the claimed theoretical grounding and interpretation of important additions unresolved, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
